This month, Google launched the all-new Pixel 11 series. Compared to last year's Pixel 10 series, the phone itself hasn't changed much, but there are many welcome improvements in terms of user experience, one of which is the addition of new camera processing options that give users more fine-grained control over the final look of their photos.

Hopefully, before the iPhone 18 Pro launches, Apple will add a similar feature.

The Pixel 11 introduces a new camera feature called "Camera Looks." It's somewhat similar to the iPhone's "Photographic Styles," letting users adjust how the camera processes photos before they press the shutter. Because the adjustments happen before shooting, it's not just a standard filter.

Like Apple, Google offers multiple preset styles, but goes a step further by letting users apply fine-grained adjustments one by one. Google has also added several new styles that fit modern smartphone photography trends, including Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal.

These styles deliberately move away from the heavily processed look typical of smartphone photos, attempting to recapture the feel of traditional photography. As the name suggests, Digi focuses on a limited dynamic range, high contrast, and grainy noise, producing results that look like they came from one of those portable point-and-shoot cameras from the 2010s.

On the other hand, Minimal goes fully low-processing, with most HDR processing disabled, making photos closer to what the phone's sensor actually captures. You can check out some sample photos on the 9to5Google website.

Of course, using ProRAW on the iPhone does reduce processing to some extent, but doing so somewhat defeats the purpose of shooting with a smartphone.

Conclusion

If Apple wants to build a phone that delivers the best camera experience right from your pocket, it has to accept that every user has different needs. "Photographic Styles" is a good starting point, but Apple should take a step further. Photography is fundamentally a form of self-expression, so giving users more choice over how much processing is applied to their photos is an important step. Apple should take a cue from Google and add a Minimal style to the iPhone.

What do you think of the iPhone's current photography performance? Do you like Apple's latest "Photographic Styles," or do you think it still falls short? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
